note: Lessons for the method modules. A lesson is exposition: it states the rules, shows how they fit, and hands off to the cards that keep them available and the problem questions that test whether they can be used. Every lesson carries its sources and a `verify` line — the app states a rule, it does not vouch for it.

lessons.title: How to study law, and why this app works the way it does
lessons.summary: Retrieval beats re-reading, a case brief is a discipline rather than a summary, and the app is built around both.

sections.h: The method matters more here than elsewhere

body.text: Law is a large volume of material that has to be recalled precisely, structured well enough to be applied to facts you have never seen, and written down under time pressure. Very few subjects need all three at once. A study method that works for a subject needing only the first will fail here, slowly, in a way you will not notice until an examination.
This lesson is about the method. It is short, and it is worth more than any single doctrine below it.

sections.h: Re-reading feels like work and is not

body.text: The most robust finding in the learning research is also the least intuitive: re-reading a text produces a strong feeling of mastery and very little durable memory. The feeling comes from fluency — the second pass is easier than the first, and the brain reads ease as knowing.
Retrieval practice beats review. Trying to recall something, and failing, does more for retention than reading it again — provided you then check the answer.
body.source: Make It Stick; the retrieval practice literature

body.text: This is why the app makes you answer a card before showing you the back, and why the problem questions make you write the whole answer before the rubric appears. Both are structured to stop you reading the answer and mistaking recognition for recall.
The corollary is uncomfortable: study that feels harder is usually working better. If your revision feels smooth and pleasant, be suspicious of it.

sections.h: Spacing, and why the intervals grow

body.text: Material reviewed at increasing intervals is retained far longer than material reviewed in a block. The app schedules cards on that principle, using FSRS, and the intervals lengthen because each successful recall makes the memory more durable.
Space your reviews, and interleave topics rather than blocking them. Mixing contract and criminal in one session feels worse and produces better discrimination between them.
body.source: Make It Stick; the spacing and interleaving literature

body.text: Interleaving matters especially in law because the hard skill is telling doctrines apart on facts that do not announce which is which. Studying tort for a solid week teaches you tort; studying tort mixed with contract teaches you to notice which one you are looking at.
Reading a judgment straight through, like an article, is the commonest waste of a student's time. A judgment is a document with a structure, and you read it by extracting that structure.

items: Facts — only the material ones. A fact is material if changing it might change the outcome.
Procedural history — which court, on appeal from what, and what was decided below.
Issue — the question of law the court had to answer, stated as a question.
Holding — the answer to that question.
Reasoning — why. This is the part worth your attention.
Ratio — the rule the decision rests on, stated so it could govern a different case.
Obiter — anything else worth noting, marked as such.

body.text: Write it down. A brief you did not write is a brief you do not have, and the act of compressing a judgment to a page is where the understanding happens. Briefs also mean you never re-read a full judgment for revision.
Do not brief from a headnote. Headnotes are written by editors, are sometimes wrong, and are never authority. Read the judgment.

sections.h: How to answer a problem question

body.text: Use IRAC, or the ILAC variant, and use it visibly. Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion.

The marks in a problem question are overwhelmingly in the Application. Students who lose marks usually state the law competently and then stop, or restate the facts without connecting them to the rule. Application means saying which fact satisfies which element, and where the difficulty is.
State the rule with its source. Apply it to these facts. Argue both sides where the point is genuinely arguable. Then answer the question that was asked.
Write under time from the beginning. An answer you could have written in ninety minutes is worth nothing in a forty-minute question, and the only way to learn the pace is to practise at it.

sections.h: What this app is and is not

body.text: Three layers. Lessons state the rules and orient you to the reading. Cards keep the rules available, scheduled so you meet them just as they start to fade. Problem questions test whether you can use them, and make you predict your own mark before you see the rubric, because a self-taught student's largest blind spot is their own judgment of their work.

What it does not do is replace the textbooks. The lessons are an orientation and say so; the depth is in the reading list, and a lesson here is roughly what a good tutorial would cover before you go away and read properly.

It also cannot mark your writing. Nothing here reads your answer. The self-mark is honest only if you are, and the app is explicit about that on the progress page rather than hiding it behind a number.

lessons.title: How a legal system is arranged
lessons.summary: Three divisions that decide, before anything else, which rules apply and who has to prove what.

body.text: Before you can ask what the law says about a situation, you have to know which body of law is being asked. A punch in a car park can be a crime, a tort, or both at once, and the answer to “what happens next” is completely different in each case — different party bringing it, different standard of proof, different remedy. Getting the division right is the first move in every problem you will ever be given, and it is invisible in a textbook because the textbook has already made it for you by putting the chapter in a particular book.
There are three divisions worth holding in your head from the beginning. None of them is difficult. All of them are the sort of thing that is embarrassing to be unsure about in the second year.

Public law governs the relationship between the individual and the State: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law. Private law governs the relationship between individuals: contract, tort, property, family, company. The dividing question is who is on each side of the dispute and in what capacity.
Public law: the State is a party in its capacity as the State. Private law: the parties meet as equals, and the State supplies only the court.
body.source: Standard classification; see Williams, Learning the Law

body.text: The division is not perfectly clean, and you should not expect it to be. A government department that breaches a supply contract is being sued in contract, as an ordinary contracting party, not in public law. The test is the capacity in which the State acts, not the fact that a State body appears on the page.
This is the division students most often blur, because the same facts frequently support both. Keep them apart by asking who is bringing the case and what they are asking for.

A criminal case is brought by the State — in Malaysia, by the Public Prosecutor — against an accused, and it asks for punishment. A civil case is brought by one party, the plaintiff, against another, the defendant, and it asks for a remedy: damages, an injunction, a declaration.
Criminal: prosecution by the State, seeking punishment. Civil: claim by a private party, seeking a remedy.

A drunk driver injures a pedestrian. The Public Prosecutor charges him under the road traffic legislation — that is the criminal case, and the pedestrian is a witness in it, not a party. The pedestrian separately sues him in negligence for her medical costs and lost income — that is the civil case, and the outcome of the criminal one does not decide it.

An acquittal in the criminal case does not defeat the civil claim, because the standards of proof are different. Failing to prove something beyond reasonable doubt is not the same as failing to prove it on the balance of probabilities.

The two standards follow directly from the division above, and the reason for the gap between them is worth understanding rather than memorising: the consequences of a wrong criminal conviction fall on one person and are close to irreversible, so the system deliberately accepts letting some guilty people go in order to make wrongful convictions rare.
Criminal: beyond reasonable doubt. Civil: on the balance of probabilities — more likely than not.
body.source: Evidence Act 1950; standard common law formulation

body.text: “Balance of probabilities” means exactly what it says: if the tribunal thinks it is more likely than not, that is enough, and 51% will do. “Beyond reasonable doubt” is not a percentage and does not become one however hard you press it. It is a state of the tribunal's mind, and the courts have generally resisted attempts to quantify it.
The last division is the one that does the most work later and gets the least attention now. A question of fact is what happened. A question of law is what the rules make of it.

It matters for three reasons, and each one will cost you marks if you have not internalised it. Appeals are often restricted to questions of law, so how a point is characterised decides whether it can be appealed at all. Precedent attaches to propositions of law, not to findings of fact, so a case is authority for its rule and never for its facts. And in a jury system the division allocated the work between judge and jury — which is historical in Malaysia, jury trial having been abolished, but it is why the distinction is drawn so sharply in the older cases you will read.
Fact: what happened. Law: what follows from it. Appeals, precedent and the division of labour in a trial all turn on which is which.

“The defendant was driving at 90 km/h” is a question of fact. “Driving at 90 km/h in those conditions fell below the standard of a reasonable driver” is a question of law, or at least a question of mixed fact and law — which is a third category, and one that is fought over precisely because so much depends on where a point lands.

You will not be examined on these divisions directly for very long. They stop being a topic and become the frame you read everything else in — which is why they are worth over-learning now, while there is time. The five cards this lesson plants are deliberately small; they are meant to be automatic rather than thought about.

When you meet a set of facts, run the divisions before you reach for any rule: public or private, civil or criminal, and which parts of the story are contested fact and which are contested law. Most misfired answers in a first year come from skipping that step.

lessons.title: What binds, and what merely persuades
lessons.summary: Stare decisis, the ratio and the obiter, and the four ways a court escapes a decision it does not want to follow.

body.text: Common law systems decide cases by reference to how earlier cases were decided. The doctrine has a Latin name — stare decisis, “to stand by things decided” — and a simple rationale: like cases should be treated alike, and people should be able to arrange their affairs knowing what the law is.
Stare decisis: a court is bound by the decisions of courts above it in the same hierarchy, on the same point of law.

Notice the three qualifications built into that sentence. Above it — precedent runs downwards. In the same hierarchy — a court in another country is in another hierarchy. On the same point of law — a case decides what it decides and no more. Almost every argument about precedent you will read is an argument about one of those three.
A judgment is a long document. Only part of it binds anybody, and identifying that part is the central skill of case reading.
The ratio decidendi is the legal principle the court's decision actually rests on: the rule applied to the material facts in order to reach the result.

The operative word is rests. The test is necessity, not emphasis or length. A judge may spend four pages on a point that turns out to be beside the point, and dispose of the decisive issue in two sentences. Whether a proposition is the ratio is answered by asking whether the outcome would have been the same without it.

A ratio stated at the level of the facts is useless. “The council is liable for the blocked drain” binds no later case, because no later case has that drain in it. You have to state the rule at a level of generality that could govern a different set of facts — and choosing that level is where the argument usually is.

Everything in the judgment that is not the ratio is obiter dictum — “a thing said by the way”. It does not bind. It may still carry great weight: an observation by the Federal Court on a point it did not have to decide is not binding, but no High Court judge will brush it aside lightly.
Obiter dictum: a statement in a judgment that was not necessary to the decision. Persuasive at most, never binding.

The clearest obiter is the kind a court flags itself: “we have heard no argument on this point and express no view upon it.” A court that expressly declines to decide something has not decided it, however suggestive the surrounding language.

The hard cases are the ones nobody flags. A court that gives two independent reasons for its result has arguably given two rationes, and later courts will disagree about whether the second one was necessary. Do not expect the line to be clean; expect to argue about where it falls.
Binding authority must be followed whether the judge agrees with it or not. Persuasive authority may be followed, and its weight depends on the court, the reasoning, and how close the facts are.
Binding: a decision of a superior court in the same hierarchy, on the same point. Persuasive: everything else — obiter, decisions of coordinate courts, decisions of foreign courts, textbooks.

A judge of the High Court is not bound by another judge of the High Court. Judicial comity means they will normally follow a decision of coordinate jurisdiction unless convinced it is wrong, but that is a convention of good practice, not an obligation.

Foreign judgments are never binding on a Malaysian court, and this is worth saying flatly because the practice can look otherwise. English, Singaporean, Indian and Australian cases are cited constantly in Malaysian courts, and sometimes followed almost as a matter of course. They are nonetheless persuasive only. A different hierarchy cannot bind this one.
A court faced with an inconvenient precedent has a limited set of legitimate moves, and knowing them is how you argue precedent rather than merely recite it.

items: Distinguishing. The earlier case turned on a material fact that is absent here, so its ratio does not reach this case. This is the everyday move and the one you will use most.
Overruling. A superior court declares the earlier decision wrong. Only a court above the one that decided it can do this — and, within limits, a final court can do it to itself.

Reversing. An appellate court sets aside the decision below in the same case. Not the same thing as overruling, though students routinely confuse them: reversing is vertical within one case, overruling is about a different, earlier case.
Per incuriam. The earlier decision was reached in ignorance of a binding authority or a relevant statute, and so does not bind.

body.text: Per incuriam: decided in ignorance of a statute or binding authority that would have altered the result. Such a decision does not bind.

Per incuriam is narrow, and it is not a licence to disregard a decision you think is poorly reasoned. The earlier court must have missed something it was obliged to consider. Bad reasoning is not enough; overlooked authority is.

This lesson plants seven cards, and they are worth being ruthless about — precedent vocabulary used loosely is the fastest way to look untrained. Then attempt the problem question, which gives you a short judgment and asks you to separate the ratio from the obiter and say what a later court is bound by. It is harder than it looks, and the passage most students mis-sort is the one that reads like an aside but was actually argued.

lessons.title: The words you cannot work around
lessons.summary: Five maxims that carry whole doctrines, and three fact cues that should trigger a doctrine before you have finished reading the sentence.

body.text: Legal Latin is not decoration and it is not gatekeeping, whatever it looks like from outside. Each of the phrases below is a compression: a single term that names a whole doctrine, so that judges and counsel can refer to it without restating it. You cannot read a judgment fluently without them, and looking each one up as it appears makes reading four times slower.

Learn them as index entries rather than translations. The point is not that you can render audi alteram partem into English; it is that seeing it makes an entire body of administrative law available to you at once.

sections.h: The five that earn their place

body.text: Ultra vires — beyond the powers. An act done outside the authority conferred by the statute or instrument that grants it, and therefore invalid.

This is the engine of judicial review and of a good deal of company law. A public body has only the powers Parliament gave it; a company, historically, only those in its objects. Acting outside them is not merely wrong, it is void.
Audi alteram partem — hear the other side. Nobody should be condemned unheard.
Nemo judex in causa sua — no one a judge in his own cause. A decision-maker must not have an interest in the outcome.

Those two together are the rules of natural justice, and they are the substance of procedural fairness in administrative law. Almost every judicial review application you read will be founded on one of them, and they are among the very few doctrines you can rely on across common law jurisdictions without checking.
Actus reus — the guilty act. The physical element of an offence: the conduct, and any required circumstances or consequences.
Mens rea — the guilty mind. The mental element: intention, knowledge, recklessness or negligence, as the offence requires.

Both criminal terms are less useful in Malaysia than a common law training suggests, because the Penal Code defines each offence with its own mental element written into the section. The vocabulary still matters for reading the case law and for talking about the structure of an offence, but do not go looking for a general doctrine of mens rea in a codified system. Read the section.

sections.h: Fact cues, and why they are worth drilling

body.text: Issue-spotting is a retrieval problem, not a reasoning problem. In a problem question the facts do not announce which body of law they belong to, and the students who do badly are usually not the ones who cannot state the rules — they are the ones who never reached for them.
So it is worth building explicit associations between a shape of facts and the doctrine it should summon. Three to begin with:

items: A promise, an exchange, and someone who has not performed → contract. Ask whether an agreement was formed, whether it is enforceable, and what the remedy is.
Someone injured, and a question of who should have prevented it → tort, and negligence first. Ask about duty, breach, causation and remoteness, in that order.
A public body making a decision that affects someone, with a defect in how it was made → administrative law, and judicial review. Ask about natural justice and about acting within power.

body.text: These are starting points, not answers, and a good set of facts will engage two or three at once. That is fine — the failure mode is engaging none.

The eight cards here are the shortest in the deck and should stay that way. If a card is taking you more than a couple of seconds it is carrying too much, and you should split it rather than keep failing it. When a maxim starts appearing in your own writing without being reached for, it has done its job.

lessons.title: The courts, and what each one can do
lessons.summary: The civil hierarchy from the Magistrates' Court to the Federal Court, the two High Courts, and the statutes that create them.

body.text: Precedent runs downwards through a hierarchy, so the doctrine you learned in the foundations module is inert until you know the shape of the structure it runs through. Everything about which decisions bind, which can be appealed, and which court can hear a matter at all follows from this diagram.

sections.h: The civil courts, lowest to highest

items: Magistrates' Court — the base of the ordinary hierarchy, handling the lower-value civil claims and the less serious criminal matters.
Sessions Court — above the Magistrates, with a higher civil limit and a wider criminal jurisdiction.
High Court — unlimited original jurisdiction, and the first of the superior courts. There are two, dealt with below.
Court of Appeal — hears appeals from the High Court.
Federal Court — the apex court of Malaysia.

body.text: Magistrates' Court → Sessions Court → High Court → Court of Appeal → Federal Court. The Federal Court is the apex.
body.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964; Subordinate Courts Act 1948

body.text: There is also the Penghulu's Court, at the very bottom, with a tiny jurisdiction and almost no practical significance today. It is worth knowing it exists so that you are not caught out by a reference to it, and not worth more than that.

The civil jurisdictional limits of the Magistrates' and Sessions Courts are monetary figures set by statute and raised periodically. Do not memorise a number from a textbook — look it up in the current Subordinate Courts Act 1948 each time you need it, because a figure you learned three years ago is likely to be wrong.
This is the fact about the Malaysian structure that most surprises people arriving from an English textbook, and it is constitutionally significant rather than administrative.
There are two High Courts of coordinate jurisdiction: the High Court in Malaya, and the High Court in Sabah and Sarawak.
body.source: Federal Constitution; Courts of Judicature Act 1964

body.text: They are coordinate, which means neither binds the other. A decision of the High Court in Malaya is persuasive in Sabah and Sarawak and no more, exactly as one High Court judge's decision is persuasive to another. The arrangement reflects the terms on which the Borneo states entered the Federation, and it is a real feature of the system rather than a quirk of naming.
The structure is not in the Constitution alone. Two Acts do the work of setting out jurisdiction, and you should be able to name both without hesitating.
Courts of Judicature Act 1964 — the superior courts: High Courts, Court of Appeal, Federal Court. Subordinate Courts Act 1948 — the Sessions and Magistrates' Courts.
body.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964; Subordinate Courts Act 1948

body.text: The division is easy to remember once you notice it tracks the superior/subordinate line exactly, which is the same line that decides whether a court's decisions can bind anybody at all.
Running alongside the civil hierarchy is a second one, with its own three tiers: the Syariah Subordinate Court, the Syariah High Court, and the Syariah Appeal Court at the top.
Syariah Subordinate Court → Syariah High Court → Syariah Appeal Court.
body.source: State enactments; Ninth Schedule, List II

body.text: Two things about it are structural rather than incidental, and both are dealt with properly in a later lesson. These are State courts, created by State law, not federal ones — so there is no single national Syariah hierarchy but a set of parallel State ones. And they are not below the Federal Court: no appeal runs from the Syariah Appeal Court to the civil courts. Two hierarchies, not one tree with a branch.

Five cards, all of them the kind of structural fact that has to be instant. Draw the diagram from memory once a week until it is dull. The reasoning that uses it comes in the next two lessons, and neither will make sense if you are still working out the order of the courts while reading them.

lessons.title: Where Malaysian law comes from
lessons.summary: The Constitution at the top, statute below it, English common law received to a date, and custom that counts as law.

body.text: It is tempting to assume the sources of law are obvious — statutes and cases — and to move on. In Malaysia that assumption will cost you, because the Constitution itself defines what counts as law and the definition is wider than a common law training expects.
Article 160(2): “law” includes written law, the common law in so far as it is in operation in the Federation or any part of it, and any custom or usage having the force of law.

Three sources, then, and the third is the one students forget. Custom is not an inferior thing that yields to statute automatically; where it has the force of law it is law, and the adat of Negeri Sembilan and the native customary law of Sabah and Sarawak are applied by the courts as such.

This is the single most important structural difference between Malaysia and the United Kingdom, and if you carry an English textbook's assumptions across you will get it backwards. The United Kingdom has parliamentary sovereignty. Malaysia does not.
Article 4(1): the Constitution is the supreme law of the Federation, and any law passed after Merdeka Day which is inconsistent with it is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
An Act of Parliament can therefore be struck down. That single sentence is what makes constitutional litigation possible at all, and it is the foundation of the fundamental liberties module later on.
Do not write that Parliament is sovereign in Malaysia. It is a common slip carried over from English texts, and it is wrong in a way that undermines everything built on top of it.

Below the Constitution sits written law: Acts of Parliament at federal level, Enactments of the State Legislative Assemblies at State level, and Ordinances in Sarawak. What each may legislate on is fixed by the Ninth Schedule, which divides subjects into the Federal List, the State List and the Concurrent List.
Parliament has two houses: the Dewan Rakyat, the elected lower house, and the Dewan Negara, the appointed and State-elected upper house.

Beneath primary legislation is subsidiary legislation — rules, regulations, orders and by-laws made by a body on which Parliament has conferred power to make them. It is law, it is enforceable, and it is where a great deal of the detail actually lives.
Subsidiary legislation: law made under authority delegated by an Act, by a minister or other body. Valid only within the powers the parent Act confers.

Its validity depends on the parent Act, which is why the ultra vires doctrine from the foundations module bites here: subsidiary legislation made beyond the delegated power is void, and challenging it is ordinary administrative law rather than constitutional litigation.

sections.h: English common law, received to a date

body.text: Malaysia is a common law jurisdiction, but the common law did not arrive by osmosis. It was received by statute, and the statute fixes a date.

Civil Law Act 1956, s 3(1): the court shall apply the common law of England and the rules of equity as administered in England on 7 April 1956 for West Malaysia, 1 December 1951 for Sabah, and 12 December 1949 for Sarawak — so far only as the circumstances of the States and their inhabitants permit, and subject to such qualifications as local circumstances render necessary.

Two things follow. First, there are three different cut-off dates, and using the West Malaysian one for a Sarawak matter is an error that a marker will see immediately. Second, English decisions after the relevant cut-off are not received. They may be cited, and they frequently are, but as persuasive reasoning rather than as law that arrived automatically.
Section 6 of the same Act excludes English land law, which matters because Malaysia has a Torrens system of registered title and the English doctrines would cut across it.

Be honest about the complication rather than hiding it. Malaysian courts cite post-1956 English cases constantly, and there is a respectable argument that a later English decision merely declares what the common law always was, which would pull it back inside the cut-off. That argument is available to your opponent. Meet it rather than pretending the date settles everything.

For an ordinary dispute, work down: is there a provision of the Constitution in play; is there a Malaysian statute on the point; is there subsidiary legislation under it; is there binding Malaysian case law; and only then, is there received English common law under s 3, subject to local circumstances.

A student asked whether a landlord may do something will often find a case first, because a case is what a search engine returns. The order above says find the Act first. A case cannot authorise what a statute forbids, and starting from the case makes it easy to miss that the question was answered by s 5 of an Act nobody looked at.

Four cards, then two problem questions that use this material hard. One asks you to choose between sources when a custom, an old English case and a modern one all bear on a matter; the other puts a Federal Court decision against a Privy Council decision and asks which binds. Both are more about knowing what a source is than about the substantive law.

lessons.title: Two court systems in one country
lessons.summary: Article 121(1A), what it actually says, and why it is not the general ouster it is usually described as.

body.text: Malaysia runs two court hierarchies side by side. The civil courts you met in the last lesson are federal, created under the Constitution and the Courts of Judicature Act 1964. The Syariah courts are State courts, created by the enactments of each State, with their jurisdiction drawn from the Ninth Schedule.
The Syariah courts have jurisdiction only over persons professing the religion of Islam, and only over the matters listed in the Ninth Schedule, List II, Item 1.
body.source: Federal Constitution, Ninth Schedule, List II, Item 1

body.text: Both halves of that sentence are limits, and both get forgotten. The jurisdiction is personal — it reaches Muslims — and it is subject-matter limited, covering Islamic personal and family law, certain offences against the precepts of Islam, and related matters. It is not a general jurisdiction over anything with a religious flavour.
In 1988 the Constitution was amended to add clause (1A) to Article 121. It is short, and it is quoted wrongly more often than almost any other provision.
Article 121(1A): the civil High Courts “shall have no jurisdiction in respect of any matter within the jurisdiction of the Syariah courts.”

Read it slowly. It is a rule about overlap. It removes civil jurisdiction over matters that are within Syariah jurisdiction — and therefore does nothing at all about matters that are not. Since Syariah jurisdiction is limited by subject and by the religion of the parties, the reach of 121(1A) is limited in exactly the same way.

The common misstatement is “if Islam is involved, the civil court has no jurisdiction.” That is not what the clause says and not what it does. A dispute involving a Muslim party is not automatically within Syariah jurisdiction, and a non-Muslim cannot be brought before a Syariah court at all.

sections.h: What the clause could not do

body.text: For roughly two decades after 1988, 121(1A) was read expansively, and civil courts declined jurisdiction in a series of cases where a party had no other forum available — including non-Muslims who could not, by definition, appear before the court they were being sent to.

The Federal Court's decision in Indira Gandhi in 2018 is the turning point, and it rests on a proposition larger than the clause. Judicial review of administrative action is inherent in the civil courts and forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution. A constitutional amendment did not remove it, and 121(1A) did not purport to.

Indira Gandhi: Art 121(1A) does not oust the civil courts' inherent power of judicial review; and the Syariah courts' jurisdiction cannot extend to a person who does not profess the religion of Islam.
body.source: Indira Gandhi a/p Mutho v Pengarah Jabatan Agama Islam Perak [2018] 1 MLJ 545 (FC)

body.text: The practical consequence is that a non-Muslim spouse or parent is not left without a forum. The civil court decides whether an administrative act was lawful; it does not decide questions of Islamic law, and it is careful to say so.

The recurring fact pattern is a marriage under the Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976 in which one spouse converts to Islam and then converts the children without telling the other. It is worth knowing the constitutional answer.

Article 12(4): the religion of a person under the age of eighteen shall be decided by his parent or guardian — read with the Eleventh Schedule, under which the singular includes the plural, so the consent of both parents is required where both are living.

That reading is what Indira Gandhi settled. It is a small piece of statutory interpretation doing a very large amount of work, which is a good illustration of why the interpretation module later in the curriculum is not an optional extra.

Two cards, and then the problem question, which puts a mother in the civil High Court against a jurisdictional objection built on 121(1A). The argument that wins is not about religion; it is about reading the clause as written and noticing that the Syariah court's own jurisdiction has limits.

lessons.verify: Indira Gandhi is the controlling authority and is cited for more than it decides. Read the Federal Court's reasoning in a report you can hold, and check whether any later Federal Court decision has qualified it before relying on the basic-structure passages.

lessons.title: Finding the law, and knowing when you have not
lessons.summary: Statute first, case second, and the citator problem that makes free Malaysian sources unsafe to stop at.

body.text: Research has an order, and almost every bad answer comes from working out of it. Search engines return cases, so cases are what you find first; but a case is evidence of what the law is, and the Act is the law.

items: Find the governing statute. Read the section, not a summary of it.
Check that the statute is current: latest reprint, amending Acts, whether an amendment has actually commenced.
Look for subsidiary legislation made under it, where the operative detail often lives.
Then find the cases, and place each one in the hierarchy — which court, what year, ratio or obiter.
Then check whether those cases are still good law.

body.text: Asked whether a landlord may distrain for rent without going to court, a student finds a High Court decision saying yes and reports it. The governing instrument is the Distress Act 1951, and it sets out a route through an application to the court. Starting from the case made it possible to miss the Act entirely.

sections.h: Where to get the text, free

body.text: The official text of Malaysian Acts is published free by the Attorney General's Chambers on its portal. That is the source to use for statute.
Free case sources exist too, and they are genuinely useful for reading a judgment. What they are not is complete, and the gap is specific rather than general.

A citator is the tool that tells you a case's subsequent history: whether it was appealed, reversed, overruled, distinguished, followed, or merely doubted. Noting up a case means running it through one.
Noting up: checking a case's subsequent judicial treatment to establish whether it is still good law.
You cannot confirm from free Malaysian sources alone that a case is still good law. There is no free citator. That check requires CLJ, LexisNexis CaseBase, or Westlaw Asia.
body.source: Practice; the constraint is commercial, not legal

body.text: The dangerous inference is the silent one. A free portal showing no overruling is not evidence that there was none — it is evidence that the portal does not track overruling. Absence of a warning is not a clean bill of health, and treating it as one is how a student advises on a case that was reversed on appeal fifteen years ago.

This is not a reason to avoid free sources. It is a reason to know precisely what they cannot tell you, and to say so when you report. An answer that states its own limits is worth more than one that quietly has them.
You will regularly be asked a question with less time than a complete check requires. Refusing to answer is not the professional response; neither is answering as though the check had been done.

The form that works: here is the governing provision and what it says; here is the case law I found and where each case sits in the hierarchy; here is what I have not been able to verify and what tool it would need; and here is what I would not advise on this basis. That is a bounded answer, and it is what the problem question in this module asks you to produce.

Three cards, which are about where to look and what the limits are rather than about any rule of law. Then the problem question, whose answer is a method rather than a proposition — the only one in the set where a correct substantive conclusion earns almost nothing if the order of work is wrong.
